name: Sulphite Railroad Bridge
facts: The Sulphite Railroad Bridge, built in 1896-7, remains the only surviving upside‑down covered railroad bridge in the United States, with the rail bed perched atop its roof to protect the trusses below.
Spanning 234 feet with a 180‑foot central Pratt truss, the bridge was engineered by the Boston and Maine Railroad to carry sulfite to Franklin’s paper mills, a key industry of the era.
After the mills closed in the 1920s, the line fell into disuse and the bridge was abandoned in 1973, leaving it vulnerable to vandalism, arson, and the harsh New Hampshire elements.
